source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Expect beta-blocker therapy to make tachycardia a more reliable warning of hypoglycemia, so pulse changes can be trusted more strongly.","B":"Teach that beta-blockers may mask some hypoglycemia warning signs, so glucose monitoring remains important when symptoms are less obvious.","C":"Teach that beta-blockers eliminate the need for glucose monitoring because clinically important hypoglycemia becomes unlikely during treatment.","D":"Expect beta-blockers to prevent hypoglycemia during exercise or missed meals, so routine glucose checks can safely be reduced."}}
source_row.rationale: Current insulin labeling notes that antiadrenergic drugs such as beta-blockers can reduce or eliminate some signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia. Option B is correct because it warns that symptom recognition may be blunted and reinforces glucose monitoring. Option A incorrectly makes tachycardia more reliable. Option C incorrectly removes monitoring. Option D incorrectly states that beta-blockers prevent hypoglycemia.
source_row.source_detail: DailyMed HUMULIN R — Drug Interactions, Drugs That May Blunt Signs and Symptoms of Hypoglycemia: antiadrenergic drugs including beta-blockers may reduce or eliminate signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia; glucose monitoring remains necessary. source_row.stem: A client with diabetes is prescribed a beta-blocker and says tachycardia is a main warning sign used to recognize hypoglycemia. What should the nurse teach?
